| [](https://substack.com/redirect/eb3cc53b-e78d-4247-803f-2bf60c502619?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
When Americans voted overwhelmingly to send Donald Trump back to the White House and deliver Republican majorities in both houses of Congress, they expected action. They expected the border to be secured. They expected the lawlessness of the Biden years to end. What they did not expect--and what they certainly did not vote for--was for a single unelected official appointed thirteen years ago by Harry Reid to have more control over our nation's immigration policy than the President, the Senate Majority Leader, and 53 Republican senators combined.

And yet, here we are.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=6729589&post_id=198381635&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MTk4MzgxNjM1LCJpYXQiOjE3NzkyMTAwNzcsImV4cCI6MTc4MTgwMjA3NywiaXNzIjoicHViLTY3Mjk1ODkiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.YyfuDs6Ct8s17LI_OwV984Gg3d8MSqWrqzU2CkJPRJg)
[Elizabeth MacDonough](https://substack.com/redirect/f330aac9-1b42-43d2-8686-976adea7d8a7?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) has struck again. The Senate [Parliamentarian](https://substack.com/redirect/097bc146-a013-4a76-b026-63dd729664d1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)--an obscure procedural referee who most Americans have never heard of--just delivered what amounts to a death blow to Republicans' $72 billion border enforcement package. According to reports, MacDonough has ruled that core provisions of the bill violate the Senate's arcane "Byrd Rule," effectively stripping out Border Patrol funding, cutting security technology allocations, eliminating screening measures, and removing $2.5 billion in DHS cash from the reconciliation package.

Let that sink in. A bill designed to secure our southern border--funding the brave men and women of Customs and Border Protection, providing the technology needed to detect illegal crossings, and paying for the detention and deportation infrastructure necessary to end catch-and-release--has been gutted by one person. Not by the voters. Not by their elected representatives. By Elizabeth MacDonough.
[Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9oZWFydGxhbmRqb3VybmFsLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.c-KUoL-9x6ZQES8ZjRreFfEl9PyFbLgfCUvbyWYHfOY?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=198381635)
Who is this woman, and why does she have more power over American border security than the Commander-in-Chief?
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/927acc1d-6468-4ab3-a1e1-f63fcb9dd144?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
MacDonough was appointed Senate Parliamentarian in February 2012 by then-Majority Leader Harry Reid, the Nevada Democrat who did more to destroy Senate comity and tradition than any leader in modern history. She has now held this position for over thirteen years--through the entirety of the Obama administration, Trump's first term, the Biden disaster, and now into Trump's second. She has become the longest-serving parliamentarian in Senate history, and increasingly, she has used that tenure not as a neutral arbiter of rules, but as a gatekeeper with an agenda.

This is not the first time MacDonough has conveniently found reasons to block conservative priorities. In June 2025, she torpedoed multiple provisions of Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill," ruling against oil and gas leasing provisions, public land sales, and reforms to Medicaid work requirements--policies central to the President's economic and energy agenda. She has repeatedly sided against Republican priorities while finding creative ways to allow Democratic spending sprees to proceed through reconciliation. The pattern is unmistakable.

But her latest ruling on the border bill takes her obstruction to a new level. According to sources familiar with her advisory opinions, MacDonough determined that funding for Border Patrol would "inappropriately fund activities" outside the Homeland Security Committee's jurisdiction. Translation: Republicans cannot use the reconciliation process to actually fund border enforcement because MacDonough says so. Never mind that illegal immigration is costing American taxpayers hundreds of billions annually. Never mind that criminal cartels are pouring fentanyl across our border, killing over 70,000 Americans per year. Never mind that voters demanded action.

Elizabeth MacDonough has decided that procedural technicalities matter more than American lives.

The $19.1 billion she stripped from Customs and Border Protection funding represents the backbone of what Republicans promised to deliver: more agents, better equipment, surveillance technology, and the detention space needed to end the Biden-era catch-and-release crisis. The $2.5 billion in DHS funding she eliminated was earmarked for critical security infrastructure. These aren't marginal policy preferences--they're the core of what Americans voted for in 2024.

Let's be clear about what reconciliation is supposed to do. It's a budgetary process designed to allow fiscal legislation to pass with a simple majority. The whole point is to prevent the tyranny of the minority--to stop a small group of senators from blocking spending and tax measures that have majority support. But MacDonough has twisted the Byrd Rule--which was intended to keep reconciliation focused on fiscal matters--into a weapon she uses to strip out any policy she personally dislikes.

This is legislative tyranny disguised as procedural neutrality.

And where is Senate Majority Leader John Thune in all of this? Hiding. Cowering behind parliamentary procedure rather than standing with President Trump and the conservative movement. Thune knows he has the power to fire MacDonough. His predecessor as Majority Leader could dismiss her tomorrow and replace her with someone who will actually follow the law rather than rewrite it. Previous parliamentarians have been fired for far less.

In 2001, Republican leaders dismissed Parliamentarian Robert Dove when they felt he was obstructing their agenda. Harry Reid himself wasn't afraid to replace parliamentary referees when they ruled against Democratic priorities. The notion that the Parliamentarian is some untouchable Oracle of Delphi is a fiction invented by Republicans who lack the courage to govern.

Thune's excuse--that overruling MacDonough would "break Senate norms"--is laughable. What about the norm that elections have consequences? What about the norm that the majority party gets to set the legislative agenda? What about the norm that securing the border shouldn't require 60 votes in a body where 53 senators represent the majority view?

The truth is simpler and more damning: John Thune doesn't want to secure the border. He wants the appearance of trying while blaming a bureaucrat for his own lack of resolve. He wants to tell voters he fought for border security while hiding behind MacDonough's skirts when it matters. It's cowardice masquerading as institutionalism.

President Trump was elected with a mandate to secure the border. Republican senators campaigned on the same promise. Yet they are allowing one person--appointed by Harry Reid during the Obama administration--to nullify that mandate with advisory opinions that have no basis in the Constitution and no democratic legitimacy whatsoever.

This cannot stand. The Senate Parliamentarian serves at the pleasure of the Majority Leader. Elizabeth MacDonough is not a constitutional officer. She is not elected. She is not accountable to the voters. And she has more than demonstrated that her loyalties lie with the Democratic Party that elevated her and the procedural obstructionism that defines Beltway governance.

John Thune needs to make a choice: Stand with President Trump and the American people who demand border security, or stand with Elizabeth MacDonough, her $171,315 taxpayer funded salary, and the permanent bureaucracy that wants to maintain the open-border status quo. He cannot do both.

If Thune continues to hide behind MacDonough's rulings, when he knows he has the power to end her obstruction, then he is complicit in the betrayal of Republican voters. He becomes an accessory to the very open-border policies he claims to oppose.

Fire Elizabeth MacDonough. Do it today. Or admit that you were never serious about securing the border in the first place.

The American people deserve leaders who lead--not politicians who look for excuses to fail.

So apparently securing the border now requires permission from someone most Americans couldn't pick out of a lineup. | | | May 19 | | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|--- When Americans voted overwhelmingly to send Donald Trump back to the White House and deliver Republican majorities in both houses of Congress, they expected action. They expected the border to be secured. They expected the lawlessness of the Biden years to end. What they did not expect--and what they certainly did not vote for--was for a single unelected official appointed thirteen years ago by Harry Reid to have more control over our nation's immigration policy than the President, the Senate Majority Leader, and 53 Republican senators combined. And yet, here we are. has struck again. The Senate obscure procedural referee who most Americans have never heard of--just delivered what amounts to a death blow to Republicans' $72 billion border enforcement package. According to reports, MacDonough has ruled that core provisions of the bill violate the Senate's arcane "Byrd Rule," effectively stripping out Border Patrol funding, cutting security technology allocations, eliminating screening measures, and removing $2.5 billion in DHS cash from the reconciliation package. Let that sink in. A bill designed to secure our southern border--funding the brave men and women of Customs and Border Protection, providing the technology needed to detect illegal crossings, and paying for the detention and deportation infrastructure necessary to end catch-and-release--has been gutted by one person. Not by the voters. Not by their elected representatives. By Elizabeth MacDonough. Who is this woman, and why does she have more power over American border security than the Commander-in-Chief? | | ---|---|--- MacDonough was appointed Senate Parliamentarian in February 2012 by then-Majority Leader Harry Reid, the Nevada Democrat who did more to destroy Senate comity and tradition than any leader in modern history. She has now held this position for over thirteen years--through the entirety of the Obama administration, Trump's first term, the Biden disaster, and now into Trump's second. She has become the longest-serving parliamentarian in Senate history, and increasingly, she has used that tenure not as a neutral arbiter of rules, but as a gatekeeper with an agenda. This is not the first time MacDonough has conveniently found reasons to block conservative priorities. In June 2025, she torpedoed multiple provisions of Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill," ruling against oil and gas leasing provisions, public land sales, and reforms to Medicaid work requirements--policies central to the President's economic and energy agenda. She has repeatedly sided against Republican priorities while finding creative ways to allow Democratic spending sprees to proceed through reconciliation. The pattern is unmistakable. But her latest ruling on the border bill takes her obstruction to a new level. According to sources familiar with her advisory opinions, MacDonough determined that funding for Border Patrol would "inappropriately fund activities" outside the Homeland Security Committee's jurisdiction. Translation: Republicans cannot use the reconciliation process to actually fund border enforcement because MacDonough says so. Never mind that illegal immigration is costing American taxpayers hundreds of billions annually. Never mind that criminal cartels are pouring fentanyl across our border, killing over 70,000 Americans per year. Never mind that voters demanded action. Elizabeth MacDonough has decided that procedural technicalities matter more than American lives. The $19.1 billion she stripped from Customs and Border Protection funding represents the backbone of what Republicans promised to deliver: more agents, better equipment, surveillance technology, and the detention space needed to end the Biden-era catch-and-release crisis. The $2.5 billion in DHS funding she eliminated was earmarked for critical security infrastructure. These aren't marginal policy preferences--they're the core of what Americans voted for in 2024. Let's be clear about what reconciliation is supposed to do. It's a budgetary process designed to allow fiscal legislation to pass with a simple majority. The whole point is to prevent the tyranny of the minority--to stop a small group of senators from blocking spending and tax measures that have majority support. But MacDonough has twisted the Byrd Rule--which was intended to keep reconciliation focused on fiscal matters--into a weapon she uses to strip out any policy she personally dislikes. This is legislative tyranny disguised as procedural neutrality. And where is Senate Majority Leader John Thune in all of this? Hiding. Cowering behind parliamentary procedure rather than standing with President Trump and the conservative movement. Thune knows he has the power to fire MacDonough. His predecessor as Majority Leader could dismiss her tomorrow and replace her with someone who will actually follow the law rather than rewrite it. Previous parliamentarians have been fired for far less. In 2001, Republican leaders dismissed Parliamentarian Robert Dove when they felt he was obstructing their agenda. Harry Reid himself wasn't afraid to replace parliamentary referees when they ruled against Democratic priorities. The notion that the Parliamentarian is some untouchable Oracle of Delphi is a fiction invented by Republicans who lack the courage to govern. Thune's excuse--that overruling MacDonough would "break Senate norms"--is laughable. What about the norm that elections have consequences? What about the norm that the majority party gets to set the legislative agenda? What about the norm that securing the border shouldn't require 60 votes in a body where 53 senators represent the majority view? The truth is simpler and more damning: John Thune doesn't want to secure the border. He wants the appearance of trying while blaming a bureaucrat for his own lack of resolve. He wants to tell voters he fought for border security while hiding behind MacDonough's skirts when it matters. It's cowardice masquerading as institutionalism. President Trump was elected with a mandate to secure the border. Republican senators campaigned on the same promise. Yet they are allowing one person--appointed by Harry Reid during the Obama administration--to nullify that mandate with advisory opinions that have no basis in the Constitution and no democratic legitimacy whatsoever. This cannot stand. The Senate Parliamentarian serves at the pleasure of the Majority Leader. Elizabeth MacDonough is not a constitutional officer. She is not elected. She is not accountable to the voters. And she has more than demonstrated that her loyalties lie with the Democratic Party that elevated her and the procedural obstructionism that defines Beltway governance. John Thune needs to make a choice: Stand with President Trump and the American people who demand border security, or stand with Elizabeth MacDonough, her $171,315 taxpayer funded salary, and the permanent bureaucracy that wants to maintain the open-border status quo. He cannot do both. If Thune continues to hide behind MacDonough's rulings, when he knows he has the power to end her obstruction, then he is complicit in the betrayal of Republican voters. He becomes an accessory to the very open-border policies he claims to oppose. Fire Elizabeth MacDonough. Do it today. Or admit that you were never serious about securing the border in the first place. The American people deserve leaders who lead--not politicians who look for excuses to fail. | | **Join Alice Walker in our fight to defeat corporate genocidal Democrat Adam Smith and elect Kshama Sawant to Congress!**

**Our campaign has an ambitious target to raise $75,000 this month and we’re over halfway there!**
[**Can you donate $25, $100, $500, or any amount to help us reach our goal?**](https://us.list-manage.com/NW9Sgzxb2h7?e=bbdb764b3a&c2id=8b3f9b08d69d5a7a0bcc2cd67f268e15)

| | Dear Peter,
Kshama for Congress is the strongest independent, antiwar campaign in the country. Our campaign has raised over $550,000 and has **more than seven times as many donors as Kshama Sawant’s warmongering opponent, Democrat Adam Smith.** We have working class donors in every city in Congressional District 9, in every state in the nation, and in Washington DC and Puerto Rico. This is because working people here and around the country want a proven fighter like Kshama in Congress to stand up against the warmongering billionaires and their political servants.
**That's also why Pulitzer Prize winning author of The Color Purple and activist Alice Walker has just endorsed Kshama Sawant:** “I am proud to support Kshama Sawant’s upcoming Seattle, WA Congressional election campaign. Her victory would mark a great advance for all who stand opposed to today’s endless US wars against working people at home and abroad.”
**We have set a target of raising $75K in May to build on our momentum and to go all out to elect the first ever revolutionary socialist to the U.S. Congress.** We raised over $6,000 in the first 24 hours since launching this fundraising drive, and are now at over $39,000 for the month of May. But to hit our target, we need to build on our momentum!
---
|
---
| | [**Can you chip in $25, $100, or $500 today to send a proven working class fighter to Congress? Donate now!**](https://us.list-manage.com/16kDWNYIBud?e=bbdb764b3a&c2id=8b3f9b08d69d5a7a0bcc2cd67f268e15)
---
|
---
| | **Kshama Sawant stands as the only consistent anti-war, pro-worker candidate in this race.** She's calling for an end to all military aid to Israel, for free healthcare for all funded by taxing the rich, to shutdown ICE and the detention centers, and for national rent control. **No other candidate in this race is fighting to end all military aid to Israel, or fighting for taxing the rich to fund free healthcare for all and a massive expansion of affordable housing.** Kshama has an unprecedented track record of building movements to win historic victories for working people, like the highest minimum wage in the country, unprecedented renters rights, and the Amazon Tax which taxes the wealthiest businesses to fund hundreds of millions of dollars of affordable housing every year.
Kshama’s opponent, Adam Smith, has been a loyal servant of the billionaires and weapons industry for 29 years. In that time, Smith has voted for trillions of dollars in U.S. military funding and he has supported war after bloody war. He voted to create and to repeatedly fund ICE, to cut Medicare and Medicaid by hundreds of billions of dollars, to fund Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and to block U.N. food aid to Gaza.
In December, Smith voted for a record-breaking $906 billion in military spending, which Trump is now using to carry out the horrific war on Iran. Just three days ago, Smith voted to pass CORCA, a bill that grants ICE and DHS more power to collect American citizens' personal information. Smith profits off of this in his campaigns, with the full backing of AIPAC, Palantir, and all the major weapons manufacturers as the #1 recipient of weapons industry money among House Democrats.
We're up against millions of dollars in this campaign, because the billionaires love Adam Smith, and the last thing they want is socialist Kshama Sawant in Congress. To win, we need you to donate and sign up to volunteer today!
---
|
---
| [DONATE TODAY](https://us.list-manage.com/Tni_hrEkC6p?e=bbdb764b3a&c2id=8b3f9b08d69d5a7a0bcc2cd67f268e15)

Help build our independent movement to shut down ICE and stop the deportations, for a $25/hour minimum wage, to end U.S. military aid to Israel, for free healthcare for all by taxing the rich, for national rent control, and for a new party for the working class!
[**Donate $25, $100, or $500 now!**](https://us.list-manage.com/BnCdkkSR0Uj?e=bbdb764b3a&c2id=8b3f9b08d69d5a7a0bcc2cd67f268e15)

We have a real shot to win this campaign, but the Democratic Party will fight tooth and nail to keep Kshama out of Congress because they know she is a real fighter for working people. We need everyone to get involved to get the word out in order to defeat them!
[**Sign up to volunteer with our campaign today!**](https://us.list-manage.com/BMW51rGhpSs?e=bbdb764b3a&c2id=8b3f9b08d69d5a7a0bcc2cd67f268e15)

There is a false binary forming around artificial intelligence, and you can feel it in political rooms.
Either you are "pro-AI," which often sounds like worshipping at the altar of tech billionaires, or you are "anti-AI," which often gets framed as the only pro-human, pro-worker, pro-planet position -- but leaves principled, ethical, forward-minded people in the dust when it comes to adopting the most powerful force-multipliers of our time.
I reject that binary.
I am not interested in becoming "the AI candidate." I am interested in being an honest candidate in a country where this technology is already here. AI is already reshaping labor, education, media, small business, campaigns, surveillance, government services, weapons systems, energy demand, and the information environment our children are growing up inside.
Congress cannot govern what it refuses to understand.
_And the people cannot afford leaders who confuse personal abstinence with public policy._
The real question is not whether AI exists. It does. The question is who controls it, who benefits from it, who pays the costs, and whether working people, families, communities, and constitutional rights have any meaningful protection as this technology spreads.
My position is simple: I am pro-humanity, pro-worker, pro-planet, pro-privacy, pro-democracy, and pro-accountability.
That is exactly why AI must be governed. Rejection will not save us. Regulation might.
* * *
Personally, I use AI carefully and ethically as a force multiplier because I am a mother of two toddlers running a grassroots campaign without corporate PAC money, foreign interests, billionaire donors, or a massive political machine. I use it to research, organize, translate, summarize, prepare, build, and stretch scarce time and scarce money.
I do not use it to harm anyone, violate privacy, fake support, impersonate people, manufacture endorsements, deepfake opponents, make moral decisions, or replace human relationships. I do nothing with it that violates the law or my personal moral code, for which I know I will answer to my Creator.
I use it the way grassroots campaigns have always used every lawful, ethical tool available: **to help ordinary people compete against entrenched, corrupt, immoral power.**
That matters, because campaigns powered by corporate PACs, defense contractors, and institutional machines already have _armies_ of consultants, staff, lobbyists, donor networks, opposition researchers, and political infrastructure working for them.
Grassroots campaigns do not.
So yes, I use tools that help a people-powered campaign survive, thrive, and **win** **with integrity**. And yes, I believe those tools need serious regulation.
Both things are true. In fact, they belong together.
Refusing to learn how a technology works does not protect workers. It does not protect children. It does not protect artists. It does not protect elections. And it does not protect the planet.
_It simply leaves the technology in the hands of the people already powerful enough to shape it without us -- and use it on us._
Abstinence is not governance.
* * *
While we're here: yes, the environmental concerns are very real.
The International Energy Agency projects that global electricity consumption from data centers could more than double by 2030, reaching around 945 terawatt-hours, with AI as a major driver. In the United States, the IEA projects that data centers will account for nearly half of electricity demand growth between now and 2030.
Water concerns are also real. The Environmental and Energy Study Institute has reported that large data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons of water per day, depending on size, cooling systems, and local conditions.
We know from on-the-ground reporting that families near data centers are dealing with brown water coming out of the taps, power loss, and massive rate hikes, for which they're receiving no financial relief or other equity -- yet another terrible and unsurprising example of privatized profits and socialized losses. This is _exactly_ why capitalism requires regulation to protect the public interest, and representing the public interest is _exactly_ what Congress is supposed to be doing.
So no, we cannot abandon our fellow Americans by waving away the climate and water costs.
We must protect each other, and _govern_ this.
That means binding transparency on data center energy and water use. It means government incentives, shifting to mandates, that corporations use _available technology_ to reduce data center space, power, and water use by over 95% by deploying [hardware with almost no latency](https://substack.com/redirect/a069f6a0-9474-4fa2-9990-c8c9ccba2ccd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg): well over 95% of compute power is dead time, on current tech. It means requiring renewable-powered buildout, grid-protection rules, and no sweetheart deals that make working families pay higher utility bills so tech giants can scale faster. It means community benefit agreements, water protections, efficiency standards, and real public accountability _before_ massive infrastructure is approved.
Every time a powerful industry wants special treatment, the democratic governance questions should be simple:
_**Who benefits?**_
_**Who pays?**_
_**Who gets a say?**_
If the answer is "the corporation benefits, the public pays, and the community gets ignored," then the answer from Congress should be **no.**
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/f384d36c-6cb1-41fe-9f16-c3d37edb8653?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
* * *
The labor concerns are real too.
AI must not become another tool for executives to deskill workers, cut wages, monitor every keystroke, automate judgment, or concentrate wealth at the top. Workers deserve bargaining power, retraining, ownership pathways, and protection from algorithmic management and workplace surveillance.
They also deserve a seat at the table before their jobs are redesigned around systems they did not choose, cannot inspect, and are not allowed to challenge.
This is where I think some of the current conversation falls short. It is not enough to say, "AI will create jobs." That sounds like a tech lobbyist talking point. Maybe some jobs will be created. Maybe some work will become easier, safer, faster, or more accessible. Maybe - and a lot of folks miss this one - AI will make it easier for neurodivergent people to contribute fully, communicate effectively, and express their gifts fully at work and in their passion pursuits. **But** -- we also know what happens when powerful tools enter an economy already designed to reward extraction.
The benefits rise. The risks and costs fall downward. Executives call it innovation and rake in the profits. Workers call it rent, groceries, childcare, and trying not to get replaced by a system they were never allowed to understand.
That is not inevitable. But it is the direction things always go when power is left alone.
Refusing to learn the technology will not save workers. It will leave this massively powerful technology in the hands of bosses, monopolies, and military contractors.
Working people need **power over AI,** not exclusion from it.
* * *
The democracy concerns may be the most urgent of all.
Synthetic media must be disclosed. Deepfakes in elections must be regulated -- or banned outright, with consequences. Government use of AI must be transparent, appealable, auditable, and constrained by due process.
**No person should be denied housing, healthcare, immigration relief, employment, benefits, parole, bail, or basic public services because an algorithm made a decision no one can explain.**
A constitutional government does not rule by black box.
That principle matters _**now**_ , before these systems become too embedded to unwind. It matters in immigration. It matters in policing. It matters in public benefits. It matters in hiring, lending, housing, education, and healthcare. It matters anywhere a human being can be reduced to a risk score, a flagged profile, or a probability estimate without a real chance to challenge the result.
Due process cannot mean "a machine said so."
Freedom cannot mean "trust the model."
Accountability cannot mean "the vendor says it works."
And we need to be especially clear about military and surveillance AI. AI _**cannot**_ become a blank check for autonomous killing, mass targeting, predictive policing, immigrant surveillance, protest monitoring, or religious, racial, or ideological profiling.
**We have already seen what happens when government power, private contractors, secrecy, fear, and profit braid themselves together.**
The result is not safety. It is a machinery of control.
This is not science fiction anymore. It is an **immediate and urgent** procurement question. It is a budget question. It is a constitutional question. It is a moral question.
And Congress has a duty to answer it BEFORE the worst actors set the default.
* * *
This is where the comparison to crypto often comes up, and I understand why.
Crypto taught us what happens when speculative technology outruns democratic accountability. Too much of it became scam-ridden, extractive, energy-intensive, and detached from real productive value.
We should learn from that.
But AI is not exactly the same thing. AI is not just a speculative asset class. It is a general-purpose capability layer. It touches education, medicine, disability access, translation, logistics, agriculture, legal navigation, small business, organizing, public administration, research, and yes, surveillance, manipulation, labor displacement, and the never-ending wars our government is so addicted to.
That means the answer cannot be hype. It also cannot be panic.
**The answer has to be** _**governance**_**.**
Use what helps people. Regulate what harms people. Democratize what concentrates power. Ban what violates rights. Tax, constrain, and condition what burdens the grid, water, workers, and communities.
That is not fence-sitting.
That is statesmanship.
* * *
I know this is a flashpoint. I know many people hear "AI" and immediately think of job loss, stolen creative work, data centers, deepfakes, plagiarism, surveillance, and the dead-eyed corporate language of "efficiency" that almost always means someone lower on the ladder is about to be harmed.
Those concerns are not irrational. They are grounded in reality.
**But the answer to abuse is not ignorance.** It is power, literacy, law, and democratic control.
_If we leave AI to the monopolies, the billionaires, the defense contractors, and the same political class that**already** let corporate power hollow out so much of American life, we should expect more of the same: more extraction, more surveillance, more concentration, more profit taken from public risk._
BUT if We the People understand the technology, organize around it, regulate it, and insist that it serve human dignity rather than replacing it, **something different remains possible.**
That is the path I care about.
Not AI as a god.
Not AI as a gimmick.
Not AI as an excuse to abandon workers, farmers, artists, teachers, students, parents, or the planet.
AI as a **tool** that must be held accountable to human flourishing.
**Technology must serve life. It must serve the people. It must serve a livable planet. It must remain under democratic law.**
No monopoly above the people.
No algorithm above due process.
No machine above moral responsibility.
That is the standard.
And it is the only serious one.

Hi, friend: I'm reaching out today to ask you to **_[chip in $5 to my campaign for governor of New Mexico.](https://act.debhaaland.com/go/8176?refcode=jtk730-fr-nd&t=2&akid=9742%2E400544%2EWOWdWE)_**
And I know what you might be thinking: _Just $5? Is that really going to make a difference?_

The answer is **_yes_**.
Every single dollar adds up — because it's not just your $5, but it's also hundreds of $5 donations in Las Cruces, in Rio Rancho, in Roswell, in Gallup, and beyond.

* * *
* * *
California's liberal experiment is costing regular people a fortune, and the bill isn't just for housing or gas anymore. It's for the whole package--the "liberal surcharge" baked into every tax dollar that funds programs sounding compassionate on paper but delivering something uglier in practice. The state takes your money, slaps on layers of bureaucracy and connected insiders, and spends it on things that push even left-leaning tolerance to the breaking point. Families are buckling. Businesses are bolting. And the exodus isn't some mystery--it's math.
Start with the basics of living here. Gas in Los Angeles is flirting with $9 a gallon in some spots, thanks to state taxes and regs that tack on about $1.50 extra per gallon compared to the national average. Groceries run 11 percent higher. Utilities 61 percent. Housing? Forget it unless you're already loaded. One study tracking movers from 2016 to 2025 found Californians who left saved $672 a month on housing alone. After seven years out, they were 48 percent more likely to own a home. That's not ideology talking. That's pocketbook reality. Yet Sacramento keeps doubling down on the one-party machine that created this mess.
Fox Business **[called it an"abusive relationship"](https://substack.com/redirect/1f11b9e5-7d4d-4b86-a5c1-10f2a3f1aa75?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** with Democratic rule, and the description fits. No checks, no moderation, just relentless policies that crush the middle class while the wealthy and connected skate. LA's GOP chair put it plain: parents commute across a massive county for jobs they can't afford near home. The only non-Democrat on the LA City Council sees it in his own grocery runs and constituents' complaints. Professor Joel Kotkin nails the dynamic--California had a thriving oil industry decades ago, now it's regulated into oblivion under Gavin Newsom. Result? High poverty rates despite all the wealth creation on paper. One-party dominance means no pushback. Orange County's 50-50 split forces some balance. Sacramento? Not so much.
* * *
* * *

P.S. She NEVER thought these files would go public (**and when you see bombshell #1, you 'll understand why.**) **[Watch now](https://substack.com/redirect/4767e73f-0cf2-4510-906c-7829fc903d65?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** before this video is scrubbed from the internet forever.
* * *
* * *
The money extracted doesn't just vanish into vague "services." It funds specific choices that test how far tolerance stretches. Take tablets in prisons. Back in 2023, the rollout looked like a tech-savvy win for rehab. California handed out about 90,000 free Android devices across its prisons.
No more lines at payphones causing fights and stress. Inmates could call family for free (with limited minutes), text, access legal resources, even meditation apps. Supporters sold it as bridging the digital divide, boosting family bonds, cutting recidivism. **[The New York Post described](https://substack.com/redirect/38722906-380f-4b06-8e04-f89d3e969ecd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** inmates streaming Hollywood hits like "Puss in Boots: The Last Wish," curating Spotify-style playlists, playing games like Football Cup or Bingo World.
Aventiv Technologies, supplying hundreds of thousands nationwide, claimed educational content would slash the 70 percent reoffending rate. **[Cap Radio quoted](https://substack.com/redirect/04affeb7-3446-4daf-be8f-03ae646ac3db?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** prisoners saying the atmosphere improved--no more frustration, more connection, even estranged siblings reconciling. It was all framed as modern rehabilitation, preparing people for release in a digital world.
Fast-forward three years. The picture is darker. Newsom's administration poured $189 million--potentially up to $315 million--into new tablets for every inmate, including death row, under the banner of "digital equity" and the California Model rehab push. No cost to the offenders themselves.
The devices were supposed to be tightly controlled education tools. Instead, **[they're personal sex machines.](https://substack.com/redirect/9eb9facd-fc54-4532-bcc3-4f8c2e39fee4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** Inmates **[stream porn](https://substack.com/redirect/9eb9facd-fc54-4532-bcc3-4f8c2e39fee4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** via 30-second video clips during calls, where outsiders play explicit content on their end. They **[trade nude photos, sext, even receive nudes](https://substack.com/redirect/9eb9facd-fc54-4532-bcc3-4f8c2e39fee4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** from the outside. Death row convicts have openly admitted it. One incarcerated serial child molester used his tablet for hours daily to **[harass a 12-year-old victim of his from inside prison](https://substack.com/redirect/9eb9facd-fc54-4532-bcc3-4f8c2e39fee4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** , grooming and soliciting more images.
A former high-level prison official described the likely scale: vast amounts of child porn circulating, thousands of minors potentially groomed. The old "reintegration" promise? Buried under reality. Taxpayers aren't funding Hamlet or job skills. They're bankrolling boundary-pushing access that even the most progressive reformer might call a bridge too far.
As for the concerns about misuse? They were dismissed. With the former deputy director of California's adult parole operations **[telling City Journal](https://substack.com/redirect/9eb9facd-fc54-4532-bcc3-4f8c2e39fee4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** that "there is no way to monitor the nearly 90,000 **[inmates](https://substack.com/redirect/713d8652-dd51-46c7-99c7-23d4f2bc8413?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** in the state prison system who have access to taxpayer-funded devices."
This is the pattern. Problems get attention only when the fix enriches the right network. **[Look at the diaper program Newsom rolled out right before Mother's Day.](https://substack.com/redirect/e7c90e91-2f8f-4527-9a22-12c325fa23db?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** Golden State Start: $20 million to deliver roughly 40 million diapers to 100,000 low-income newborns--about 400 per kid, or roughly a month's supply for a newborn using 10 to 12 a day. On the surface, hard to knock. But dig in. The state pays 50 cents per diaper through a Los Angeles nonprofit called Baby2Baby. Walk into any Target and the same everyday packs go for about 16 cents each. Three times cheaper.
## [Gavin Newsom's diaper scandal blowout](https://substack.com/redirect/e7c90e91-2f8f-4527-9a22-12c325fa23db?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

The cash doesn't go straight to parents or stores either. It routes through Baby2Baby, which handles distribution via hospitals. The co-CEO since 2011 sits on the board of the California Partners Project, co-founded and run by Jennifer Siebel Newsom, the governor's wife. That same project helped broker the partnership. Roughly two-thirds of the $20 million around $13.6 million never bought an extra diaper. It lines connected pockets instead. Families get the product. Insiders get the contract and the cut. Everyone else gots the invoice.
The consequences stack up for regular people. High costs driven by misspent taxes **[are driving the exodus from the Left Coast.](https://substack.com/redirect/2d2b2da8-8c4e-4989-8c03-f909cf787aa1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)** It's no longer just families packing U-Hauls. It's structural. Starbucks, a Seattle icon tied to progressive roots, is dropping $100 million into a new corporate office in Nashville, creating up to 2,000 jobs. Washington's business tax climate cratered from sixth-best to 45th.
Silicon Valley Tech billionaires like Zuckerberg, Brin, and Page have shifted billions to Miami where luxury home sales there are surging. Companies vote with their headquarters the same way individuals vote with their feet. Lost revenue means even bigger holes in state budgets, which gets papered over with more fees, more regs, more surcharges just to keep the same (corrupt?) game rolling and the cycle accelerates.
## [The "Left Coast" exodus just makes good financial sense](https://substack.com/redirect/2d2b2da8-8c4e-4989-8c03-f909cf787aa1?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)

California treats its citizens like an endless ATM for ideological experiments and insider deals. The liberal attitude that once sold itself as enlightened now delivers porn tablets for death row, triple-priced diapers routed through the governor's wife's network, and policies that make basic life eye wateringly expensive. Families feel mugged at the pump, in the grocery aisle, and on their tax returns. Businesses see the writing on the wall and leave. The state keeps promising solutions while the practical impact on regular Californians gets worse. This isn't sustainable.

Spencer Pratt is popular for a reason, and it's not just because of his epic campaign videos.

That's not ideology talking. That's pocketbook reality. Yet Sacramento keeps doubling down on the one-party machine that created this mess. Fox Business with Democratic rule, and the description fits. No checks, no moderation, just relentless policies that crush the middle class while the wealthy and connected skate. LA's GOP chair put it plain: parents commute across a massive county for jobs they can't afford near home. The only non-Democrat on the LA City Council sees it in his own grocery runs and constituents' complaints. Professor Joel Kotkin nails the dynamic--California had a thriving oil industry decades ago, now it's regulated into oblivion under Gavin Newsom. Result? High poverty rates despite all the wealth creation on paper. One-party dominance means no pushback. Orange County's 50-50 split forces some balance. Sacramento? Not so much. Sponsored by: | | ---|---|--- Nancy Pelosi 's worst nightmare is happening RIGHT NOW... have just been leaked online... And the revealed inside have the entire Swamp QUAKING. Because they 've been kept under government lock and key for more than 55 YEARS. Until today. P.S. She NEVER thought these files would go public (and when you see bombshell #1, you 'll understand why.) before this video is scrubbed from the internet forever. The money extracted doesn't just vanish into vague "services." It funds specific choices that test how far tolerance stretches. Take tablets in prisons. Back in 2023, the rollout looked like a tech-savvy win for rehab. California handed out about 90,000 free Android devices across its prisons. No more lines at payphones causing fights and stress. Inmates could call family for free (with limited minutes), text, access legal resources, even meditation apps. Supporters sold it as bridging the digital divide, boosting family bonds, cutting recidivism. inmates streaming Hollywood hits like "Puss in Boots: The Last Wish," curating Spotify-style playlists, playing games like Football Cup or Bingo World. Aventiv Technologies, supplying hundreds of thousands nationwide, claimed educational content would slash the 70 percent reoffending rate. prisoners saying the atmosphere improved--no more frustration, more connection, even estranged siblings reconciling. It was all framed as modern rehabilitation, preparing people for release in a digital world. Fast-forward three years. The picture is darker. Newsom's administration poured $189 million--potentially up to $315 million--into new tablets for every inmate, including death row, under the banner of "digital equity" and the California Model rehab push. No cost to the offenders themselves. The devices were supposed to be tightly controlled education tools. Instead, Inmates via 30-second video clips during calls, where outsiders play explicit content on their end. They from the outside. Death row convicts have openly admitted it. One incarcerated serial child molester used his tablet for hours daily to , grooming and soliciting more images. A former high-level prison official described the likely scale: vast amounts of child porn circulating, thousands of minors potentially groomed. The old "reintegration" promise? Buried under reality. Taxpayers aren't funding Hamlet or job skills. They're bankrolling boundary-pushing access that even the most progressive reformer might call a bridge too far. As for the concerns about misuse? They were dismissed. With the former deputy director of California's adult parole operations that "there is no way to monitor the nearly 90,000 in the state prison system who have access to taxpayer-funded devices." This is the pattern. Problems get attention only when the fix enriches the right network. Golden State Start: $20 million to deliver roughly 40 million diapers to 100,000 low-income newborns--about 400 per kid, or roughly a month's supply for a newborn using 10 to 12 a day. On the surface, hard to knock. But dig in. The state pays 50 cents per diaper through a Los Angeles nonprofit called Baby2Baby. Walk into any Target and the same everyday packs go for about 16 cents each. Three times cheaper. | | | | ---|---|--- | May 13 | The cash doesn't go straight to parents or stores either. It routes through Baby2Baby, which handles distribution via hospitals. The co-CEO since 2011 sits on the board of the California Partners Project, co-founded and run by Jennifer Siebel Newsom, the governor's wife. That same project helped broker the partnership. Roughly two-thirds of the $20 million around $13.6 million never bought an extra diaper. It lines connected pockets instead. Families get the product. Insiders get the contract and the cut. Everyone else gots the invoice. The consequences stack up for regular people. High costs driven by misspent taxes It's no longer just families packing U-Hauls. It's structural. Starbucks, a Seattle icon tied to progressive roots, is dropping $100 million into a new corporate office in Nashville, creating up to 2,000 jobs. Washington's business tax climate cratered from sixth-best to 45th. Silicon Valley Tech billionaires like Zuckerberg, Brin, and Page have shifted billions to Miami where luxury home sales there are surging. Companies vote with their headquarters the same way individuals vote with their feet. Lost revenue means even bigger holes in state budgets, which gets papered over with more fees, more regs, more surcharges just to keep the same (corrupt?) game rolling and the cycle accelerates. | | | | ---|---|--- | Apr 23 | California treats its citizens like an endless ATM for ideological experiments and insider deals. The liberal attitude that once sold itself as enlightened now delivers porn tablets for death row, triple-priced diapers routed through the governor's wife's network, and policies that make basic life eye wateringly expensive. Families feel mugged at the pump, in the grocery aisle, and on their tax returns. Businesses see the writing on the wall and leave. The state keeps promising solutions while the practical impact on regular Californians gets worse. This isn't sustainable. Spencer Pratt is popular for a reason, and it's not just because of his epic campaign videos. It's Gary Sinise here. You may know me from my roles in movies like Apollo 13 _ _ and The Green Mile or the CBS television series CSI: NY - but it was in 1994 playing the role of Lt. Dan in Forrest Gump that changed my life and inspired my enduring connection to our defenders, veterans, and first responders. Fellow Conservative,
_
**What happens when reliably red states start slipping away?**

We’ve seen it before, the other way around: **In 2016, Trump flipped Michigan and Wisconsin. In 2024, he took Nevada for the first time in two decades.**

Democrats didn’t have a contingency plan, and they paid for it.

But, what if the script flips and puts Republicans in the hot seat?

Recent polls show **Texas, Mississippi, Alaska, Georgia, and North Carolina — long-time Republican strongholds** — are all at serious risk of flipping or becoming highly competitive this November.

**If we lose even one or two of these firewall states, Republicans cannot afford to lose a single additional seat.

That’s why I’m asking you to support my race in Minnesota** — a race that could quietly become one of the most important insurance policies for keeping the Senate majority.

As a former Navy SEAL, I don’t believe in hoping for the best. **I prepare for the worst and fight to win.** With your help, we can flip this seat, double the number of SEALs in the U.S. Senate, and give our party critical reinforcements no matter what happens in the South or the Far North.

clean_body: When all else fails, that’s when it pays off to have a very, very good insurance policy. | Fellow Conservative, What happens when reliably red states start slipping away? We’ve seen it before, the other way around: In 2016, Trump flipped Michigan and Wisconsin. In 2024, he took Nevada for the first time in two decades. Democrats didn’t have a contingency plan, and they paid for it. But, what if the script flips and puts Republicans in the hot seat? Recent polls show Texas, Mississippi, Alaska, Georgia, and North Carolina — long-time Republican strongholds — are all at serious risk of flipping or becoming highly competitive this November. If we lose even one or two of these firewall states, Republicans cannot afford to lose a single additional seat. That’s why I’m asking you to support my race in Minnesota — a race that could quietly become one of the most important insurance policies for keeping the Senate majority. As a former Navy SEAL, I don’t believe in hoping for the best. I prepare for the worst and fight to win. With your help, we can flip this seat, double the number of SEALs in the U.S. Senate, and give our party critical reinforcements no matter what happens in the South or the Far North. That’s why I’m writing today: Every dollar will be used to protect and expand our Senate majority — even if some of our traditional strongholds fall. | | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw

Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18] | | | | | | Donald Trump just did it again. _Written with Bruce Dickson._
Last week, President Trump made his first state visit to Beijing since 2017 - two days covering trade, tariffs, Taiwan, Iran, artificial intelligence, and the future of the most consequential relationship in the world.
The summit produced agricultural commitments, 200 Boeing planes, new trade and investment bodies, a framework both sides are calling "strategic stability." It also produced something Beijing didn't have to negotiate for at all: a public signal from President Trump that Taiwan's security is a bargaining chip.
Trump left Beijing on Friday declaring "fantastic trade deals" and calling Xi Jinping ["a man I respect greatly -- really a friend."](https://substack.com/redirect/68414a41-1534-4781-8370-0791b5dadb4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) When Chinese state media was asked whether Xi considered Trump a friend, the Foreign Ministry replied with a detached boilerplate: "the two sides exchanged views on major issues." Xi does call someone his "[best friend](https://substack.com/redirect/68414a41-1534-4781-8370-0791b5dadb4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)," though. That someone is [Vladimir Putin](https://substack.com/redirect/ec7c5c45-4591-4199-b22d-0a67bd56d256?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), who arrives in Beijing [today](https://substack.com/redirect/1c371edc-1480-4825-bdd4-53d296ef0acf?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg).
Xi will visit the White House on September 24 -- coinciding with the UN General Assembly. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the two leaders are expected to meet[ as many as four times](https://substack.com/redirect/ca1ddf05-7f72-4dd5-b04e-d56b18ba462f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) this year, with APEC in Shenzhen in November and the G20 at Doral in December still on the calendar.
If you enjoy my geopolitical commentary, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Your support helps me continue producing clear, independent analysis on the global events shaping our world.

# The Deal
The ask was Beef, Boeing & Beans. Here's what the White House says came out of Beijing:
* China agreed to buy at least[ $17 billion](https://substack.com/redirect/1c8678a8-5af8-41cc-b1cb-2b0621974254?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in U.S. agricultural products annually through 2028
* China will purchase [200 Boeing planes](https://substack.com/redirect/90ba9fef-b0b1-4299-8fb2-940f3093aa5d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) and over 400 GE aerospace engines (ask was 500+ planes)
* Renewed registrations for more than 400 U.S. beef facilities and resumed poultry imports
* A new Board of Trade and Board of Investment to manage the relationship
* A 90-day tariff truce extended

That sounds great at first. But read the fine print and it's not all as it seems.
China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi confirmed after the summit that the Boeing deal isn't actually done.[ "Working teams of both sides are still discussing the relevant details."](https://substack.com/redirect/38c2e4fb-c0ac-48df-828c-354c51bc8bc4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) China never publicly confirmed a specific plane count. As a result, Boeing shares fell 3.8% Friday since investors had expected 500 planes and got an unconfirmed 200 instead.
The agricultural numbers tell a similar story. The[ $27 billion](https://substack.com/redirect/45905e94-45d9-4e7c-9b7c-639d0b4a8bc9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in combined agricultural purchases is roughly what China was already buying in 2024, before the trade war. During the trade war, that number collapsed to $8.4 billion. What Trump is calling a breakthrough is closer to a return to baseline.
The two sides'[ official readouts don't match](https://substack.com/redirect/1c8678a8-5af8-41cc-b1cb-2b0621974254?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg). China's statement didn't mention rare earths or confirm soybean volumes, and flagged tariff cuts the U.S. readout didn't mention. Trump told reporters tariffs weren't discussed. China's Commerce Ministry said both sides reached a preliminary agreement to reduce some of them. Both governments are telling their domestic audiences a different version of what was agreed.
China's Commerce Ministry called the current results[ "preliminary."](https://substack.com/redirect/45905e94-45d9-4e7c-9b7c-639d0b4a8bc9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) The Board of Trade would cover tariff relief on roughly[ $30 billion](https://substack.com/redirect/4d945f91-345f-49b1-b0fb-1cc335aa2c2b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) in goods. That's less than 10% of total U.S.-China trade in 2025.
It's also worth remembering that Trump's[ 2017 Beijing trip](https://substack.com/redirect/4d945f91-345f-49b1-b0fb-1cc335aa2c2b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) produced a commitment from China Energy Investment Corporation to invest nearly $84 billion in West Virginia shale and manufacturing. That deal dissolved entirely as tensions rose.
None of this means the summit failed on the economic front. Stability has value and the tariff truce holds. The relationship has a process now with boards, scheduled summits, and working groups. As [Nomura's chief China economist](https://substack.com/redirect/0a18ad71-f1e0-4b1d-8dc9-a9260789dc10?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) put it, the two powers have decided that "if they must be rivals, they will at least be predictable, transactional, and tightly managed rivals."
But it's not the "fantastic trade deals" Trump described boarding Air Force One. And notably, this was[ organized by Treasury Secretary Bessent](https://substack.com/redirect/68414a41-1534-4781-8370-0791b5dadb4b?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), not Secretary of State Rubio -- a breach of protocol that told you everything about what kind of summit this was designed to be. Every U.S.-China summit since Nixon has been organized by the Secretary of State. This one was built for commerce.
# Taiwan
On Air Force One, Trump called a pending[ $14 billion package](https://substack.com/redirect/e35ed043-daf2-4fec-91f9-42bfd7c2e3f5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) of missiles, anti-drone equipment, and air-defense systems a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing. He said he was "holding that in abeyance" and that it "depends on China." He added: "I'm not looking to have somebody go independent and, you know, we're supposed to travel 9,500 miles to fight a war."
Worth noting what makes that remarkable: Trump spent months pressuring Taiwan to spend more on its own defense. Taiwan's legislature voted for $25 billion in special funding for two U.S. weapons packages. Now Trump is using the weapons he pushed Taiwan to buy as leverage with the country Taiwan is arming against.
The Taiwan Relations Act -- passed by Congress in 1979 -- legally requires the United States to provide defensive military technology to Taiwan. Every president since Carter has complied. No president before Trump has ever debated or discussed with Beijing whether to do so.
According to[ Axios](https://substack.com/redirect/5b941aca-7a3f-4a97-a477-1732d1f54a71?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg), close advisers to the president privately believe the summit heightened the danger of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan within five years. One told Axios that Xi is "trying to move China to a new position where he's saying: 'We're not a rising power. We're your equal. And Taiwan is mine.'" The same advisers flagged that the U.S. chips supply chain won't be anywhere near self-sufficient if Taiwan becomes a live conflict zone...

Annual paid subscribers will receive a digital copy of my 2008 memoir, Trump's meeting with Xi proved that Taiwan's security is now a bargaining chip | | | May 19| | | ∙| | Preview ---|---|--- | | | | | | | | | | | | Written with Bruce Dickson. Last week, President Trump made his first state visit to Beijing since 2017 - two days covering trade, tariffs, Taiwan, Iran, artificial intelligence, and the future of the most consequential relationship in the world. The summit produced agricultural commitments, 200 Boeing planes, new trade and investment bodies, a framework both sides are calling "strategic stability." It also produced something Beijing didn't have to negotiate for at all: a public signal from President Trump that Taiwan's security is a bargaining chip. Trump left Beijing on Friday declaring "fantastic trade deals" and calling Xi Jinping When Chinese state media was asked whether Xi considered Trump a friend, the Foreign Ministry replied with a detached boilerplate: "the two sides exchanged views on major issues." Xi does call someone his "," though. That someone is , who arrives in Beijing . Xi will visit the White House on September 24 -- coinciding with the UN General Assembly. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the two leaders are expected to meet this year, with APEC in Shenzhen in November and the G20 at Doral in December still on the calendar. If you enjoy my geopolitical commentary, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Your support helps me continue producing clear, independent analysis on the global events shaping our world. The Deal The ask was Beef, Boeing & Beans. Here's what the White House says came out of Beijing: China agreed to buy at least in U.S. agricultural products annually through 2028 China will purchase and over 400 GE aerospace engines (ask was 500+ planes) Renewed registrations for more than 400 U.S. beef facilities and resumed poultry imports A new Board of Trade and Board of Investment to manage the relationship A 90-day tariff truce extended That sounds great at first. But read the fine print and it's not all as it seems. China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi confirmed after the summit that the Boeing deal isn't actually done. China never publicly confirmed a specific plane count. As a result, Boeing shares fell 3.8% Friday since investors had expected 500 planes and got an unconfirmed 200 instead. The agricultural numbers tell a similar story. The in combined agricultural purchases is roughly what China was already buying in 2024, before the trade war. During the trade war, that number collapsed to $8.4 billion. What Trump is calling a breakthrough is closer to a return to baseline. The two sides'. China's statement didn't mention rare earths or confirm soybean volumes, and flagged tariff cuts the U.S. readout didn't mention. Trump told reporters tariffs weren't discussed. China's Commerce Ministry said both sides reached a preliminary agreement to reduce some of them. Both governments are telling their domestic audiences a different version of what was agreed. China's Commerce Ministry called the current results The Board of Trade would cover tariff relief on roughly in goods. That's less than 10% of total U.S.-China trade in 2025. It's also worth remembering that Trump's produced a commitment from China Energy Investment Corporation to invest nearly $84 billion in West Virginia shale and manufacturing. That deal dissolved entirely as tensions rose. None of this means the summit failed on the economic front. Stability has value and the tariff truce holds. The relationship has a process now with boards, scheduled summits, and working groups. As put it, the two powers have decided that "if they must be rivals, they will at least be predictable, transactional, and tightly managed rivals." But it's not the "fantastic trade deals" Trump described boarding Air Force One. And notably, this was, not Secretary of State Rubio -- a breach of protocol that told you everything about what kind of summit this was designed to be. Every U.S.-China summit since Nixon has been organized by the Secretary of State. This one was built for commerce. Taiwan On Air Force One, Trump called a pending of missiles, anti-drone equipment, and air-defense systems a "very good negotiating chip" with Beijing. He said he was "holding that in abeyance" and that it "depends on China." He added: "I'm not looking to have somebody go independent and, you know, we're supposed to travel 9,500 miles to fight a war." Worth noting what makes that remarkable: Trump spent months pressuring Taiwan to spend more on its own defense. Taiwan's legislature voted for $25 billion in special funding for two U.S. weapons packages. Now Trump is using the weapons he pushed Taiwan to buy as leverage with the country Taiwan is arming against. The Taiwan Relations Act -- passed by Congress in 1979 -- legally requires the United States to provide defensive military technology to Taiwan. Every president since Carter has complied. No president before Trump has ever debated or discussed with Beijing whether to do so. According to, close advisers to the president privately believe the summit heightened the danger of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan within five years. One told Axios that Xi is "trying to move China to a new position where he's saying: 'We're not a rising power. We're your equal. And Taiwan is mine.'" The same advisers flagged that the U.S. chips supply chain won't be anywhere near self-sufficient if Taiwan becomes a live conflict zone...
